items.title: Jake Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: There was Menza, Romano — he was the biggest wise guy of them all

ctx.x: There were some good players that came out of there. Romano and —

Oh, the wise guys. The upstate upstarts, yeah. There was Menza, Romano — he was the biggest wise guy of them all — then Larry Covelli, Sal, Sammy Noto. They were real — Sal Nestico, Joe Romano, boy he’s a real wise guy. He worked with Gap Mangione, Chuck’s older brother you know, playing the piano and Gap, playing the piano. Joe takes a handkerchief and he throws it right across the keyboard like this. “What the hell is that for?” “Illegal use of the hands.” A real wise guy. “Watch out man, I used to be a fighter…
him. Buddy Rich loved Joe Romano. Anybody that was a real quick wit he loved. But Joe could blow you know, Joe’s a hell of a player.

items.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997
items.q: And while we were there Jake Hanna came in. And Jake went over and gave him a hug

ctx.x: I really enjoyed your perspective on him because—

It’s different from what you — I mean it’s unreal. When he was in the hospital I remember going to see him. I was on my way to Europe and Chuck Findley and I and Joe Romano to see him. We had a ride to the airport so we stopped at UCLA and this was just after his operation, and his left arm was gone, his left arm was totally paralyzed. We never saw him again. He had died while we were in Europe and his left arm was paralyzed. And he’d be laying there. And every time he’d yawn, his arm would raise. There was…
